summary: Pretend fire-tower cupola built on a Concord stone warehouse when it became a museum; now atop a private commercial office.

facts.design: Green cupola on the roof, built as a pretend fire tower with a radio, a sighting map and a two-story mural on the stairs
facts.status_note: A decorative cupola on a roof, not a working lookout

access.note: Sits atop a commercial office on the upper floors of the former museum building; access depends on the tenant

events.note: Stone warehouse built for hardware merchant David Warde; the cupola came much later
Granite Investment Advisors opened offices on the third and fourth floors, where the cupola now sits

evidence.supports: Cupola placed on the roof during museum construction, as a pretend fire tower
evidence.quote: As part of the construction of what became the Museum of New Hampshire History, a green cupola was placed atop the roof as a clever way to celebrate New Hampshire’s long history with logging and forestry, creating a pretend fire tower.

evidence.supports: Warehouse built in 1870 for David Warde
evidence.quote: It was built in 1870 as a warehouse for hardware merchant David Warde
whose retail store was on Main Street
including some years as a restaurant

evidence.supports: Building empty by the early 1990s and bought by the Historical Society
evidence.quote: By the early 1990s, it was empty, victim of a national real estate crunch, and the Historical Society sensed an opportunity.

evidence.supports: Top two floors for a museum, bottom two for collections and administration
evidence.quote: They bought the stone warehouse with the idea of using the top two floors for a museum and the bottom two for collections and administration.

evidence.supports: Radio and sighting map inside the cupola
evidence.quote: For authenticity, it included a radio and an Osborne Fire Fighter, a map with rotating sighting apertures that lets fire spotters determine the compass direction of smoke
the stairs leading up to it were decorated with a two-story mural depicting the outdoors

evidence.supports: Museum ran for about two decades
evidence.quote: for two decades it was part of the Museum of New Hampshire History

evidence.supports: Society decided two public buildings were not the way to go
evidence.quote: having two public buildings was not the way to go

evidence.supports: Museum closed and top two floors put on the commercial market
evidence.quote: So they closed the museum and listed the top two floors on the commercial market

evidence.supports: Granite Investment leased the third and fourth floors
evidence.quote: It leased the third and fourth floors

evidence.supports: Granite Investment opened offices in November 2015
Cupola sits atop the private office; principal uses it for calls
evidence.quote: the green cupola atop Lesko’s office

evidence.supports: Principal would walk up the fire tower to take calls
evidence.quote: I have a cordless headset and will walk up the fire tower sometimes to take a call

evidence.supports: Visitors still arrive thinking it is a museum
evidence.quote: A fair number of people come by thinking it’s still a museum

evidence.supports: Tenant lets visitors up depending on how busy the office is
evidence.quote: Depending on how busy we are, we’ll let them wander up

evidence.supports: Forest Lookouts lists it as a rooftop cab replica, standing
evidence.quote: Merrimack Eagle Square (Replica) 43.20682 -71.53551 Rooftop Cab Standing

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Forest Lookouts list shows the cupola as Standing, while the Monitor describes it as a pretend fire tower on a roof. The record keeps status replica, since the cupola was built as a decoration rather than as a working lookout.

sources.title: The neatest office in Concord has a fire tower – sort of

notes_for_editor: The only source on the cupola's present state is a July 2016 Concord Monitor article, so re-check the tenancy and access before relying on the 'today' paragraph. No source dates the cupola itself; the article places it in the museum conversion, which followed the early-1990s purchase. The Monitor calls the sighting device an 'Osborne Fire Fighter'; lookout sources use 'Osborne Fire Finder', so the story avoids the name. The Forest Lookouts status 'Standing' is a county-list shorthand for a roof cab; the record keeps replica.
